analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from helping or staying neutral during union organizing drives.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced with 5 cosponsors and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, it received no markup or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends a labor law section that makes it illegal for employers to give "things of value" to unions, and adds "organizing assistance" to that definition. That would make it unlawful for an employer to sign a neutrality agreement — a promise to stay neutral during an organizing drive or to recognize a union once a majority of workers sign authorization cards — or to provide any help to employees trying to organize. Today such agreements are legal and are a common way workers win union recognition without a contested election; this bill would shut that path down.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who want to avoid unionization gain the most. The bill removes the legal tool workers use most often to get an employer to the table voluntarily: a neutrality or card-check agreement, where the employer agrees not to campaign against the union and to recognize it once most workers sign cards. With that option off the table, employers could return to fighting every organizing drive, and workers would be left only with the slower, more adversarial NLRB election process. Management-side law firms and anti-union consultants also gain, since contested campaigns are where their services are sold.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, employers may voluntarily sign neutrality agreements or recognize a union when a majority of workers sign authorization cards, letting workers organize without a drawn-out, contested election campaign.

The bill adds "organizing assistance" to the definition of a "thing of value" that employers are prohibited from providing to unions under Section 302 of the Labor Management Relations Act, which would outlaw that cooperation.
The bill's title states its purpose directly: to prohibit neutrality agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Workers trying to form a union pay. Neutrality agreements are often the only realistic path to union recognition, because employer opposition during NLRB elections is common and can drag organizing campaigns out for months or years. Banning employer cooperation means workers must win a contested election against an employer free to run an anti-union campaign, which lowers union win rates and delays or defeats organizing. Union membership brings wage and benefit premiums to the workers who achieve it, so blocking the path blocks those gains.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argue workers deserve a secret-ballot election: card-check recognition means a union can be certified on the basis of signed cards with no private vote, so individual workers' final choice is never independently verified.

The bill's prohibition would apply through Section 302, a provision that carries criminal penalties, and "organizing assistance" is defined broadly as any help to employees exercising organizing rights; a definition that sweeping could chill ordinary, lawful dealings between employers and unions, not just neutrality agreements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit of the bill, if passed, would go to employers: they could no longer be asked to remain neutral, and every organizing drive would default to a contested election they can fight. The cost falls on workers, who would lose the most effective voluntary route to union recognition and face management campaigns instead. The stated benefit to workers — protecting a secret-ballot election — is real but narrow, and it is outweighed by the loss of the neutrality path that in practice is how many organizing drives succeed. The bill also invites overreach: attaching criminal-penalty liability to a broadly defined category of "organizing assistance" risks sweeping in routine employer-union conduct.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 5 cosponsors, referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Good (R-VA) introduced the bill on February 1, 2023, joined by Reps. Miller of Illinois, Perry, and Gaetz.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which was the only committee referral it received.
Five Republican House members cosponsored the bill.
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed in law, so workers kept the existing right to pursue neutrality and card-check agreements and employers gained nothing. The closest comparison: had the bill advanced, employers resisting unions would have been the winners, so the absence of action left working people where they were rather than worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers kept their organizing rights; nothing changed

for.name: Rep. Bob Good
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit neutrality agreements on February 1, 2023.

for.name: 5 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 5 cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the House majority
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote in two years.

sides.party_line_note: No floor votes occurred, but the bill's entire recorded support came from Republicans — a sponsor and 5 of 224 House Republican cosponsors, with no Democratic support — and even the Republican-led committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would let employers refuse neutrality agreements and card-check recognition without consequence, forcing every organizing drive into a contested election the employer can fight. Workers lose the most common voluntary route to union recognition, which historically carries wage and benefit gains.

industries.industry: Management-side labor consultants and anti-union law firms
industries.note: With neutrality agreements banned, every organizing campaign would default to an adversarial election fight, the market for employer-side campaign consulting. Their gain comes directly from making organizing harder for workers.

Neutrality agreements and card-check recognition are a core organizing tool; banning employer cooperation would sharply raise the cost and difficulty of winning new members. Union interests in this bill run alongside the workers they organize.
